description: A six-member team of undergraduate students in Mechatronics Engineering, Networking & IT Security, and Computer Science at Ontario Tech University and The University of British Columbia. We are united by the drive to develop innovative, data-driven solutions to further understand our world - past, present, and future.
summary:
MOSAIC (MODIS-VIIRS Observation Synthesis for Activity and Intensity Calendars) is an interactive web application that brings together over two decades of satellite fire observations into a unified platform, providing users with a consistent and accessible understanding of burning activity across Canada.

By harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data, MOSAIC accounts for differences in satellite detection capabilities, allowing historical and modern fire activity to be compared more meaningfully. Users can explore detected hotspots through an interactive map, visualize historical burning patterns through colour-coded calendars spanning weeks, months, and years, and access valuable insights such as historical trends, anomalies, and 7-day outlooks.

The platform also offers downloadable CSV/Excel datasets and predefined user viewpoints tailored to emergency responders, scientists, land managers, and firefighters, helping transform complex satellite observations into actionable information for research, environmental monitoring, and emergency preparedness.
details:
What is it and what does it do?

MOSAIC (MODIS-VIIRS Observation Synthesis for Activity and Intensity Calendars) is built upon data harmonization, which accounts for differences in MODIS and VIIRS satellite detection capabilities. By analyzing overlapping satellite observations, our team identified an overall calibration factor in our back-end development, supported by monthly adjustments to account for seasonal variations. Applying these adjustments to historical MODIS observations allowed us to create a more consistent, VIIRS-equivalent historical fire activity record, enabling more meaningful comparisons across different years.

When accessing MOSAIC, users can select their geographic region, preferred time range, and professional viewpoint before entering either the map view or calendar view. The platform includes five predefined viewpoints: General, Emergency Response, Scientists, Land Managers, and Firefighters. Each viewpoint emphasizes relevant measurements, visualizations, and suggested actions tailored to different professional needs.

The user is then free to explore satellite-detected hotspots, navigate between provinces, and click individual detections to view information such as fire classification where available, detection date and time, satellite source, confidence level, Fire Radiative Power (FRP), and suggested action items. A satellite data toggle allows users to switch between raw MODIS, raw VIIRS, and harmonized activity to visualize differences between the sensors. On the calendar, users can find colour-coded hotspot activity across weeks, months, and years, alongside interactive historical trends, seasonal patterns, regional comparisons, and anomaly indicators that highlight differences from historical averages and medians.

Beyond historical analysis, MOSAIC offers a "Predictive Outlook" breakdown using historical seasonal patterns to provide forward-looking activity estimates that support preparedness planning, as well as a page explaining the back-end process of the MODIS-VIIRS data harmonization process.

Finally, users can further filter geographic and historical data, explore detailed analytics, and download selected hotspot observations as CSV/Excel files for independent analysis.

What benefit does it have?

MOSAIC offers several benefits.

A consistent long-term fire activity record post-transition: MODIS will nearing the end of its operational use in 2027. Without harmonization, the handover to VIIRS would appear as a major jump in fire activity and break the historical record. By harmonizing this data, we are preserving the value of over two decades of satellite fire activity records.

Faster situational awareness: The burning activity calendar, anomaly colours, and percentile status let someone judge in seconds whether current conditions are normal. This replaces manual data sifting and GIS work.

Lower barrier to entry: The tool needs no GIS expertise, software installation, or coding. Anyone with a browser can query decades of satellite data.

Data transparency and reproducibility: Downloadable CSV/Excel files, raw and harmonized data comparisons, and documented methodologies allow users to independently conduct further analyses and build upon the project's findings.

What is the intended impact?

Short term:

Giving necessary parties such as early warning and emergency response teams a consistent baseline for recognizing when a region skews from its normal fire pattern. Help communities and decision makers understand fire seasons in terms they can act on.

Long term:

Preserving continuity of the fire activity records as the satellite fleet changes, so that climate-driven shifts in fire season length, timing, and intensity can still be measured. This also contributes towards raising public fire literacy by showing how fire activity is seasonal, variable, and changing, and by being clear about what satellite hotspots can and cannot tell us.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?


We developed our project as a web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no frameworks, and Leaflet for the interactive map. The fire data comes from NASA FIRMS and combines MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS detections. To make the two sensors comparable, we calculated calibration factors from the years that both sensors operated and then applied them to produce a single continuous record. We then utilized Microsoft Power BI for data extraction, analysis, and visualization, helping us interpret satellite observations and identify patterns in fire activity. We used Visual Studio Code as our editor, Git and GitHub for version control and collaboration, and GitHub Pages to deploy the app. We brainstormed in Miro, tracked tasks in Notion, and used Claude to help refine parts of our code.

How is the project creative?

MOSAIC's creativity lies in making the complex scientific process of satellite data harmonization interactive and accessible to users with different professional backgrounds. We designed persona-driven viewpoint settings that answer multiple group’s main questions in seconds. Our platform offers multiple view modes to switch between depending on what your goal is with the web app.

In addition, most fire tools show only one sensor’s data. We showcase the harmonization itself with a toggle between MODIS, VIIRS, and the harmonized series, plus the overlap period highlighted. Users can quickly toggle between the two and compare and contrast themselves to understand the difference in coverage.

The burning activity calendar feature offers a quick “activity at a glance” view that users can use to quickly see what the activity over time looks like. It also allows users to dive deeper into the data and view the data from a narrower timeframe.

What factors did your team consider?

Scientific and Data Factors

Sensor differences: Differences in spatial resolution, detection sensitivity, satellite overpass times, and day/night coverage between MODIS and VIIRS.

Harmonization method: Calibration using overlapping satellite observations, including an back-end scaling factor and monthly adjustments to account for seasonal differences in detection capabilities, such as colder weather in the winter.

Data quality: Confidence filtering, removal of persistent heat sources (gas flares, industrial sites, volcanoes), and handling of duplicate or adjacent detections.

Baseline definition: Median vs. mean, which reference period to use, and how to keep the baseline fair when the sensor mix changes within it.

Known limitations: Hotspots are not burned areas, cloud and smoke cover can hide fires, satellites have revisit gaps, and small or short-lived fires can be missed.

Technical Factors

Data volume: Processing over two decades of satellite observations across Canada requires efficient data handling. Region by region rendering keeps queries fast and specific to the users needs.

Reproducibility: Downloadable CSV/Excel files.

Human and Design Factors

Dedicated users for different users: Dedicated views for the general public, emergency responders, scientists, land managers, and firefighters, each emphasizing relevant information, visualizations, and suggested action items.

Simplicity and Usability: An intuitive default view that presents essential information at a glance, while allowing users to explore more detailed hotspot measurements, historical trends, and regional comparisons when needed.
